transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-09
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Anya Ruiz (Redwood SE), Ravi Kapoor (NexaHealth CTO), Sofia Ruiz (NexaHealth ML Eng), Ben Torres (NexaHealth Infra), Maya Singh (Product)

Summary (auto):
Quick sync on week 2 POC benchmark results. Redwood presented latency and throughput comparisons vs the baseline provider (CloudProviderX). Discussed Git: KV cache priming impact, batch sizing, quantization profile (int8), and cost tradeoffs. Agreed to run extended 2k-context tests with pre-warmed caches and to exchange prompt set. Action items captured.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Laura Chen: Okay great uh good afternoon everyone thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Ravi Kapoor: Hi, Ravi here.
[00:08] Sofia Ruiz: Sofia.
[00:09] Ben Torres: Ben.
[00:10] Maya Singh: Maya.
[00:12] Laura Chen: And from Redwood it's Laura, Marcus, Anya. All right, we'll jump in. We booked 45 minutes so plenty of time.
[00:20] Marcus Patel: Cool, I'll start with the bench results deck. Important to call out the test harness: we used the customer's sample workload that Sofia sent over, same seed prompts, 256-token responses average, and compared Redwood hosted runtime configured with int8 quantization and KV cache enabled vs your baseline cluster on CloudProviderX with their standard endpoint.
[00:37] Sofia Ruiz: Quick question, that was with the 512-batch or the 128?
[00:40] Marcus Patel: These first runs were 128 token batch size — I mean batch count 16, per-request tokens averaged 256. Sorry mixing terms.
[00:45] Laura Chen: (laughs) yeah the classic batch/tokens mixup.
[00:48] Marcus Patel: No worries. So p50 latency: Redwood median was 82ms per token, baseline was 140ms per token. p95: Redwood 230ms, baseline 680ms. Throughput wise, end-to-end requests per second at steady state: Redwood sustained 120 req/s at 256-response avg; baseline saturated at ~55 req/s before latency spiking.
[01:15] Ravi Kapoor: Wait, can you repeat the p95 numbers? 230 vs 680?
[01:18] Marcus Patel: Yeah 230ms p95 for Redwood, 680ms p95 for baseline. This was with KV cache priming on Redwood; baseline didn't have a comparable persistent cache in that setup.
[01:28] Ben Torres: How was the cache primed? We were worried about cold starts affecting our real world.
[01:31] Marcus Patel: Good call, Ben. We primed with a rolling window of the last 1000 prefixes from your transaction logs so hit rate was about 62% during the test. We can provide hit-rate over time plots.
[01:43] Sofia Ruiz: 62% is better than I expected. Does that correlate strongly to p95 improvement?
[01:47] Marcus Patel: Yes; when the KV cache hits, p95 drops dramatically because we avoid full attention recompute for those tokens. We also used kernel selection tuned for 2x longer sequences than your current median which helps tail behavior.
[02:00] Maya Singh: Can you explain the quantization impact? We saw a note about int8 causing slightly more hallucinations in earlier experiments.
[02:07] Anya Ruiz: Sure. We ran both fp16 and int8 runs. Int8 gave ~1.9x throughput increase and reduced cost, p95 improved by about 18% vs fp16 in Redwood runtime due to reduced memory pressure and better kernel packing. In our evaluation on your golden outputs set the mismatch rate (semantic delta) was within your acceptance threshold for 94% of prompts; a few edge cases we flagged.
[02:33] Ravi Kapoor: Whoa 94% is OK but we need to see the edge cases. Sofia can you lead on marking them?
[02:38] Sofia Ruiz: Yep I'll annotate which prompts caused divergent outputs and share.
[02:41] Marcus Patel: Important to note baseline provider was running fp16 and didn't have the same kernel optimizations or continuous batching we used. That explains part of the throughput delta.
[02:52] [00:03:00] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[02:54] Ben Torres: For the baseline you said they saturated at 55 req/s — what was the GPU type and containerization?
[02:58] Marcus Patel: Baseline used a single-node A100-style instance with generic server, not tuned for kv-cache, running an off-the-shelf serving stack. Redwood used a 4-GPU shard with our continuous batching and kernel selection, and the network hops were reduced by colocating the model shards with the serving fabric.
[03:15] Ravi Kapoor: Okay, so it's not apples-to-apples hardware but more of a production comparison vs our current self-managed stack. That makes sense.
[03:21] Laura Chen: Correct — think of this as what you could expect if you switched to Redwood hosted with optimizations in place. We also included a Dedicated config estimate in the appendix if you want similar performance in VPC.
[03:31] Maya Singh: How did you measure token cost? I need a clear per-1M-token cost for budgeting.
[03:35] Marcus Patel: We provided a normalized unit cost in the sheet: with int8, KV cache hit-rate at 62%, your effective per-1M-token cost on Redwood-hosted came to $12.80 vs baseline quoted $18.90 (their standard billed model). Those numbers include amortized infra and our runtime overhead.
[03:52] Sofia Ruiz: Is that including egress/data transfer?
[03:54] Marcus Patel: Egress is excluded; that's purely compute token cost. If egress is material we'll add a line item.
[03:58] Ravi Kapoor: Can you also show cost sensitivity to cache hit rate? If hit rate drops to 30% our costs go up a lot?
[04:03] Marcus Patel: Absolutely — we ran sensitivity curves: at 30% hit rate cost is about $16.50 per 1M tokens; at 80% hit rate it drops to $9.40. We'll share the CSV.
[04:13] [00:04:20] Laura Chen: Quick interjection on SLA/uptime questions that Ben raised in the first week: Redwood hosted has 99.9 uptime for production endpoints and our Dedicated tier supports SLA add-ons. Ben, any remaining open infra questions?
[04:27] Ben Torres: Yes two things: encryption-at-rest with customer-managed keys and ability to run in our VPC for sensitive PHI data.
[04:33] Anya Ruiz: Both supported. Our Private deployment can run in your VPC and integrate with KMS/HSM for key management; we also provide audit logs routed to your SIEM. We should schedule a SecOps session.
[04:44] Ben Torres: Great. Please send the SOC2 and encryption docs.
[04:47] Laura Chen: We'll include the compliance packet with the follow-up.
[04:50] [00:05:10] Sofia Ruiz: Back to the bench: any anomalies or jitter we should watch?
[04:53] Marcus Patel: There was one observed tail spike at 38 minutes into the run correlated with a garbage-collection cycle on the baseline node; Redwood's runtime isolates GC impact better. Also note we disabled autoscaling during steady-state numbers to measure single-config throughput; with autoscale Redwood can absorb spikes gracefully with failover to a lower-cost variant.
[05:13] Ravi Kapoor: Autoscale — are there warm pools or cold starts? We can't tolerate 2s cold starts for customer-facing features.
[05:18] Marcus Patel: We support warm pools and instant burst capacity. Cold starts for a fully cold shard are sub-second for small models and low single-second for larger sharded models; we can provision warm instances for critical paths to ensure sub-200ms response for the first token.
[05:32] Maya Singh: Can we have a canary rollout to test quality differences between fp16 and int8?
[05:36] Laura Chen: Definitely—our rollout supports traffic splits and automatic rollback if eval metrics drift beyond thresholds. We can help configure the canary.
[05:43] [00:06:00] Speaker 2: (paper shuffling)
[05:45] Marcus Patel: One other note: baseline's serving stack didn't support structured tool calls we were testing; that caused additional latency in their pipeline due to external orchestration. Redwood's function-calling path stays in-process where possible which reduces hop latency.
[06:00] Sofia Ruiz: We do use function calls heavily for record retrieval; good to know.
[06:04] Ravi Kapoor: Any privacy differences? We need to guarantee data isn't cached across customers.
[06:08] Anya Ruiz: KV cache is per-customer; we maintain tenant isolation. For Private deployments it's under your control. We'll add a short technical note on tenancy isolation.
[06:17] Ben Torres: Do you have examples of similar health customers and regulatory constraints?
[06:22] Laura Chen: We have a couple of customers in regulated spaces; we'll anonymize case studies and include the compliance artifacts in the follow-up pack.
[06:30] [00:06:50] Marcus Patel: Next proposed step from the SRE side: We should run a 2k-context long-sequence benchmark with KV pre-warm at different hit rates (30/60/80%) to see tail behavior and memory consumption. We'll also include an fp16 vs int8 head-to-head with the golden outputs diff.
[06:48] Sofia Ruiz: That's exactly what we want. Also can you include per-route latency (tooling vs generation) so we can model SLAs per endpoint?
[06:55] Marcus Patel: Yes, per-route breakdown included.
[06:58] [00:07:10] Laura Chen: Any questions on timeline? We're aiming to deliver the extended bench and the compliance packet by Friday, 2025-04-11. Does that work?
[07:04] Ravi Kapoor: Works for us.
[07:06] Maya Singh: Works.
[07:07] Ben Torres: Fine.
[07:09] [00:07:30] Laura Chen: Alright we'll recap: Redwood runs extended bench (Marcus), share raw logs and hit-rate plots; Sofia shares prompt set (customer); Laura shares pricing and compliance docs; schedule security deep-dive.
[07:22] Sofia Ruiz: One small item — while running the tests we noticed occasional tokenization mismatch between baseline and Redwood for a small subset of UTF-8 punctuation. Might be tokenizer versioning.
[07:32] Marcus Patel: Good catch. We'll normalize tokenization in the harness and re-run diffs.
[07:36] [00:08:00] Speaker 3: (laugh)
[07:37] Laura Chen: That's it from our side unless anyone has blockers?
[07:40] Ravi Kapoor: No blockers; thanks for the clear numbers. Appreciate the cache sensitivity curves.
[07:44] Maya Singh: Thank you.
[07:45] Ben Torres: Thanks team.
[07:47] Laura Chen: We'll follow up with the artifacts and next meeting invite — proposing same time next week for a status sync after the 2k benchmarks.
[07:55] [00:08:20] End of transcript
